Basically, the whole process gets really complicated, but both parties have super delegates. The republicans just don't have a name for them, and unbind them from the will of the state at a different point in the convention process.

Example:

Currently there are 2472 delegates, and to win, Trump needs 1237. So, if Trump doesn't get at least 1237 delegates before the convention, he may not win the nomination, even though he got more votes than any other candidate (Rule 40d). So for the sake of explanation, lets say that such an event happens:

  1. Convention has it's first vote. Most states have all their delegates bound to the results of the primary / Caucus, and is what most republicans expect to happen in the convention. Some states however (like Colorado) don't have bound delegates, because they didn't have a presidential preference poll at their Primary / Caucus. These people are for the most part the same as democratic super delegates. They can vote however they want, and most people see them as a big F-U to the people. Colorado has interesting reasons behind this, but I am not familiar with the other state's reasons.

  2. After the first round of voting, Trump emerges with a Plurality but not a Majority of delegates. Meaning, he has more delegates than Cruz or any other candidate, but he has less than the 1237 needed to win. Thus, Trump does not win the nomination, and the Republicans now have a "Brokered Convention" a.k.a. contested convention, or open convention. Rule 40e is enacted.

  3. The chairman of the convention now acts as a broker to try to reach a consensus on who the party will nominate for the national presidential election. This now means that some state's delegates become unbound and can work with eachother and the chairman to change their vote to try to pick a candidate who will get the majority. So, many of the previously bound delegates (~2/3 of the total delegate count) become unbound and can vote for whomever they like in round 2. These people are pretty much like democratic super delegates at this point, but the rules for who and how many delegates become unbound is up to the states and is not controlled by the party as a whole (This is part of the reason why Colorado has 100% unbound delegates this year).

  4. Round 2 of the voting happens, and Trump still doesn't have a Majority of the votes. THINGS GET WERID NOW

  5. In round 3, more delegates become unbound (again by state rules). Delegates continue to discuss among themselves how to resolve this deadlock. This can include strange outcomes LIKE NOMINATING SOMEONE THAT WAS NOT IN THE PRIMARIES and is what people are murmuring about right now. Some people are worried that neither Cruz nor Trump can pull enough undecided voters to win against the democrat's nomination, and even if they did, they may damage the party next election just like Bush did. So the delegates could get together and pick an entirely new candidate that is more palatable. Paul Ryan has been floated around as a name, since he was palatable enough to replace Boehner when they were gridlocked then.

  6. Many rounds continue to happen until someone (read: anyone) gets a Majority of votes.

So in a sense only democrats have super delegates who are by party rules unbound before the convention, but Republicans do have some unbound delegates from the start, and if the convention is not decided in one vote (like it was for Romney), then the Republicans have even more unbound delegates than the democrats.

TL;DR "Super Delegates" is a term that refers to democrats, but republicans have essentially the same thing due to a really complicated nomination process. So, in the event that Trump doesn't get 1237 delegates, the Republicans are going to have far, far more super delegates than the democrats.

Since a lot of people are only taking about democratic super delegates and not the republican process, many people are confused of totally unaware of how delegates are bound to candidates.

The republican party recently made a rule that says all the delegates are bound (for round 1 of voting) to the candidates that the state picks. EVEN IF THAT CANDIDATE HAS WITHDRAWN FROM THE RACE. Since Colorado voted for Rick Santorum in 2012 even though he has withdrawn before the vote, our delegates still had to vote for him at the convention. If these states were free to change their delegate's votes at round one, Romney might not have had a majority, and a different candidate may have actually won against Obama. Because of this, Colorado (and a few other states) said that they would get around the rule by simply not having a presidential vote. That way the delegates are unbound from the start and aren't tied to a candidate who has already dropped out.

This year, since Rubio has >0 delegates, trump has to get far more than 50% of the delegates to avoid a brokered convention. And since some states bind their delegates for more than one vote, we may get through multiple rounds of voting if a large number of delegates don't change candidates in round 2. And since Trump and Cruz are very divisive people, this is a definite possibility.
